description: RED, from symptom to cause. Starts with the four golden signals and descends into the subsystem explaining each one. Everything is read from recording rules, not recomputed per panel. For what the system holds rather than how it is behaving, see the product dashboard: /d/memory_mcp-product.

panels.description: Requests per second answered 5xx. The availability signal: a 5xx is a request the service failed to serve, whatever the client sent. Read against the traffic panel beside it — a high rate on a quiet service and a low rate on a busy one are different problems.
panels.title: Server errors

panels.description: The 95th percentile of request duration across every route, taken as the worst route rather than an average of percentiles. Averages of percentiles are not percentiles: one slow endpoint among many fast ones is exactly the case an average hides.
panels.title: p95 latency

panels.description: Requests per second served, whole service. Traffic is the denominator every other rate here is really a fraction of, and a sudden drop is its own incident: nothing is arriving.
panels.title: Traffic

panels.description: Server errors over all requests. The figure an SLO is written against. A 0.1% ratio on a busy service is more failures than a 10% ratio on a quiet one, which is why the rate is beside it rather than instead of it.
panels.title: Error ratio

options.content:
Four numbers, and they answer one question: **is the service working?**

- **Server errors** — requests that failed. If it is red, go to the *Traffic and errors* row.
- **p95 latency** — slow is a failure too, and often the earlier one. If it is yellow while errors are green, the service is degrading rather than broken.
- **Traffic** — a sudden collapse is its own incident, and no error panel will show it: a service receiving nothing fails nothing.
- **Error ratio** — errors as a fraction of what arrived, which is what an SLO is stated in.

Everything below explains one of these four. Read top to bottom until something is non-zero, then stop — you have found it.

panels.description: Traffic per route, five-minute rate. A route is the router's own pattern with path parameters collapsed, so this is bounded by what the server declares — and a path parameter's value never reaches a label.
panels.title: Requests per second, by route

panels.description: Failures per second, split by status class. `4xx` and `5xx` are kept apart on purpose: a `4xx` is very often the service working correctly — an unauthenticated request, a bad id — and folding it into one error number makes a healthy service look broken.
panels.title: Responses by status class

panels.description: p50, p95 and p99 per route, plus the service-wide worst. Read the gap between p50 and p99: a wide gap means a minority of requests is very slow, which is a different problem from everything being uniformly slow.
panels.title: Latency percentiles over time

panels.description: The same percentile, one line per route. This is the panel that answers *which* endpoint — every line here is a router pattern, so a slow line names the endpoint rather than a class of requests.
panels.title: p95 by route

panels.description: Requests currently being served. The saturation signal, and an honest one: the gauge is raised when a request enters a handler and lowered when it leaves, so a scrape only sees a non-zero value when it happened to land inside one. **A flat zero is the normal case and is not evidence of an idle server** — read it as 'no request was in flight at the instant of the scrape'.
panels.title: Requests in flight

options.content:
It is raised with `+1` on entry to a handler and `-1` on the way out, with no `await` in between.

A scrape has to land in that window to see anything. For a service handling a request per second, most scrapes miss.

What it *does* tell you, correctly:
- A value that never leaves zero across many scrapes, while traffic is non-zero, means requests are fast enough to miss the window — not that the server is idle.
- A value that *sticks* above zero across consecutive scrapes means requests are slow enough to be caught, and the number is how many were in flight at once.

So: read the trend across scrapes, never a single sample. CPU and memory are not exported by the application, on purpose: they are host and container figures, read from node_exporter and cAdvisor on their own dashboards, and duplicating them into this exposition would put two copies of a number in two places to keep in sync.

panels.title: Why this gauge is mostly zero

panels.description: Whether the last scrape of `job="memory_mcp"` succeeded: 1 answered, 0 did not. `up` is generated by the collector, not by the service, so this panel reads **No data** where no scrape configuration is installed (`observability/vmagent/vmagent.yml` or `observability/prometheus.yml`) — No data means 'not collected', which is not the same as healthy.
panels.title: Scrape up

panels.description: One line per scraped instance. A drop to 0 is a failed scrape, not a slow request: the collector could not reach `/metrics` at all, and every other panel on this dashboard is blind while it stays there. A *gap* rather than a zero means the collector itself was not running — the target may have been fine the whole time.
panels.title: Target up over time

panels.description: The version this exposition was built from, collapsed to one series per version — so a rollout in progress shows both versions rather than one blended figure, and a deploy that did not take is visible as a number that never moved. The value is a marker (always 1); the label is the payload, so the panel shows the label.
panels.title: Build version

panels.description: Lease and task scheduler passes, by outcome. `degraded` is its own value and means the pass itself succeeded while some tenant's step was refused — neither a failure of the pass nor a healthy one, and the reason it is not folded into `ok`.
panels.title: Scheduler passes by outcome

panels.description: Passes that failed or degraded, per scheduler. A steady non-zero line here is a subsystem that has been failing quietly for a while.
panels.title: Unhealthy passes

panels.description: How long one pass takes. Timed from when the job started running, not when it was scheduled, so queue wait is not counted as work.
panels.title: Job duration p95

panels.description: The HTTP runtime refusing to serve: a quota registry that could not be reached, a lease that could not be released, a tenant runtime that would not activate. These answer `5xx` with a generic body, so a client is told nothing and the log line's request id is the only way their report reaches an operator. Counted at the one point every warning passes through, so both logging entry points are counted exactly once.
panels.title: Refusals by operation

panels.description: Tenant namespaces reconciliation found wrong: registered but unbound, or bound to nothing. One increment per affected namespace per pass, and a pass runs at most once a minute — so a non-zero rate is a standing inconsistency, not a transient.
panels.title: Registry reconciliation

panels.description:
The identity callback declining a sign-in, by reason. Branches are a fixed set — state mismatch, nonce, id token, missing code, provider error, and `signup_invite_only`.

**These are refusals only.** A successful sign-in is not counted, so this cannot be read as a success rate, and the panel below says so rather than inviting that reading.
panels.title: Refusals by branch

options.content:
The sign-up gate answering `403`, and the one branch that is a *configuration* fact rather than a fault.

A deployment with `MEMORY_MCP_HTTP_SIGNUP_MODE=invite_only` and no invitation issued refuses every self-service sign-up — correctly, and indefinitely. Anyone seeing this branch has usually found the chicken-and-egg: the administrator door is the way in, and provisioning the first account through it is a one-time step.

**A rise here is not an outage.** Every other branch on the left is worth investigating; this one means either an attack, or a deployment whose policy closed without anyone noticing.

panels.description:
Where a memory operation spends its time, stage by stage. The five measured stages are the embedding provider, the vector index, extraction and the store write.

An operation's total says *that* something is slow. This says *which part* — and the candidates need different fixes: a slow embedding provider is someone else's problem, a slow vector index is the index, a slow store write is the database.
panels.title: Stage latency p95

panels.description: The total, per operation, for comparison with the stages beside it. A stage that accounts for nearly all of the total is the stage to look at; a set of stages that each account for a little is a different kind of slow.
panels.title: Operation latency p95

panels.description: Claim projection and reconciliation, by stage and outcome. Outcomes worth watching are `supersession` and `contradiction`: a rise in either means the knowledge graph is finding claims that disagree, which is the policy working rather than failing.
panels.title: Claim pipeline events

panels.description:
Claim relations currently stored, across schema and outcome. A level, read as it stands.

**This under-reports.** A series only exists once it has been set at least once, so a schema with no relations of some outcome is absent from the exposition rather than zero. A sudden drop in the total is real; a missing contribution is not a measurement.
panels.title: Active relations

panels.description:
Candidates considered for one claim slot, averaged.

A **mean, deliberately** — the family is exported as a summary, so a quantile would read zero for both 'no candidates' and 'a handful', which is the exact distinction this number exists to show. A rising mean means reconciliation is scanning more to place each claim.
panels.title: Mean candidates per slot

panels.description: How long a claim reconciliation pass takes. Recorded for the `reconcile` stage; projection is fast enough not to need a panel.
panels.title: Reconciliation latency p95

panels.description:
Whether the watcher backend exhausted its retries.

**A one-way latch.** Once this reads 1 it stays 1 for the process lifetime — the retry loop has returned and nothing can set it back. A dashboard that averaged it would report a fraction of a broken deployment; this reads the value as it stands. A `1` means filesystem ingestion is off and knowledge from the inbox has stopped arriving.

Exported from watcher startup, so a running watcher reads `0` and reads *No data* only when no watcher ever started.
panels.title: Watcher degraded

panels.description: Inbox files processed, by outcome. This is the product's automatic ingestion path: a rising `failed` count is knowledge that stopped arriving, and nothing else in this deployment says so.
panels.title: Revisions by outcome

panels.description: Retries while processing a revision, by the stage that failed and why. `timeout` is a single revision exceeding its attempt limit; the failure classes separate a bad file from an unreachable store.
panels.title: Retries by stage and reason

panels.description: How long one revision takes. A single revision may run to its attempt timeout, so the upper percentiles can sit well past the last reported bucket — a high number here is often a timeout, not a slow success.
panels.title: Revision latency p95

options.content:
`memory_fs_watch_queue_depth` is deliberately absent from this dashboard.

It is set **once**, at startup, from a recovery pass, and never updated again. It is a snapshot of what was queued when the process started, not the queue as it is now — a backlog that has been growing for an hour is invisible in it, and a panel showing it would invite exactly the wrong conclusion.

There is no live backlog gauge in this build. The honest signal for a stuck queue is the retry and degraded panels in the row above.

*These series exist only when the build carries `fs-watch` **and** the deployment set `MEMORY_INGESTION_INBOX`. Without both, the panels are empty — which reads as 'off', not 'broken'.*

panels.title: Queue depth is not a backlog

options.content:
All figures come from recording rules in `observability/recording_rules.yml`, so a derived number is computed once per interval rather than once per panel refresh. Every family is described at its source in `crates/memory-mcp/src/shared/observability.rs`, and each description names the trap that family has.

**The four that will mislead you if read naively:**

1. `memory_operation_results_total` counts work produced. Its `rate()` is meaningless; `increase()` over a window is the question. The product dashboard uses it that way.
2. `memory_operation_stock` and `memory_claim_relations_active` are levels, set rather than accumulated, so they are read as they stand.
3. **Every histogram is exported as a summary, not as buckets** — there is no `le` label, and latency is read from the `quantile="…"` lines. Configuring buckets would switch the exporter process-wide and cost every duration metric its quantiles.
4. `4xx` is not availability. It is very often the service working correctly.

**Known gaps, deliberately:**

- No process metrics (RSS, CPU, uptime). They are host and container figures, not application ones: read them from node_exporter and cAdvisor on their own dashboards, and use the *Saturation* row here for what the application itself can saturate on.
- `up` and `memory_build_info` come from the collection layer rather than from a request — `up` is generated by the collector and exists only where a scrape configuration is installed, and the build stamp is written once at startup. Both are on the *Collection health* row.
- No cross-tenant label. It would be unbounded; the tenant fingerprint lives in the logs instead.
